name: Design a Collaborative Document Editor
intent: Let many people type in the same document at once, see each other's changes almost instantly, and always end up with exactly the same text, even after losing the connection.
codeTitle: operational transformation of two simultaneous edits
finalIntro: Two people editing the same sentence at the same moment.
prompt: Design a real-time editor like Google Docs. Up to a hundred people can open one document and type in it at the same time. Everyone sees the others' edits and cursors within a fraction of a second, no one's typing is lost, and everyone's copy is identical at the end.
functional: Edit the text of a document, with each keystroke appearing immediately for the person typing
See other people's edits and cursors live
Keep every copy of the document identical once all the edits have arrived
Work offline for a while, and merge when the connection returns
Undo your own changes, and browse and restore earlier versions
nonFunctional: Local typing feels instant: the editor never waits for the server to show a character
Other people's edits show up within about 100 to 300 ms
Convergence: all copies end up identical, with no lost or garbled edits
Durable: a saved edit survives server crashes
Scale to millions of open documents, each with a small number of active editors

firstAttempt.text: The editor holds the document in the browser. Every few seconds, or on Save, it sends the whole text to the server, which overwrites the stored copy. To see others' changes, the page asks the server for the latest copy at intervals and replaces what is on screen.
limits: Two people editing at once overwrite each other: the last save wins and the other person's work vanishes
Replacing the text on screen moves the cursor and loses what you just typed
Changes show up only after the next save and the next poll, which takes seconds
Sending the entire document for a single keystroke is slow for big documents
A save that fails, or a lost connection, loses everything typed since the last one

steps.title: Send small edits over a live connection
steps.problem: Saving whole documents is slow and clumsy, and polling shows other people's changes seconds late.
steps.fix: Each editor keeps a WebSocket (a connection that stays open, so either side can send at any time) to a gateway. A keystroke becomes a tiny operation such as 'insert H at position 4', which is sent at once to the document server. The server forwards each operation to everyone else with the document open. The editor shows your own typing immediately, without waiting for the server.
steps.tradeoff: Edits reach others in a fraction of a second and cost a few bytes each, and nothing is replaced under the cursor. Because everyone applies the edits locally, two edits that cross on the way can now disagree about the text, which the next step fixes.

steps.title: Transform concurrent edits so every copy converges
steps.problem: Alice inserts at the start while Bob deletes the last letter. If each applies the other's operation as written, Bob's 'delete position 2' hits the wrong letter on Alice's screen and the copies end up different.
steps.fix: With operational transformation, the server gives every operation a place in one order. Before an operation is applied to text that has already changed, it is rewritten against the operations it did not know about: 'delete position 2' becomes 'delete position 3' after an insertion earlier in the text. Rules for each pair of operation types, plus a fixed tie-break when two edits hit the same position, guarantee that every copy reaches the same result. CRDTs reach the same goal by giving every character a unique, ordered identity instead.
steps.tradeoff: No edit is lost and all copies converge, while each person still types without waiting. Transformation rules are famously hard to get right for rich text, and a CRDT avoids a central ordering at the price of carrying extra data with every character.

steps.title: Give each document one owner server
steps.problem: Transformation needs one agreed order of operations per document, and editors of the same document sitting on different servers would not have one.
steps.fix: Route everything for one document to the same document server, chosen by a hash of the document id with consistent hashing, through a router in front of the gateways. That server is the single sequencer for the document (the one place that decides the order): it numbers the operations, transforms them and broadcasts them, holding the live state in memory. Different documents live on different servers, so the system scales by adding servers.
steps.tradeoff: Ordering is trivial and fast because it happens in one place, and the load is spread by document. A single very popular document is limited by one server, and if the owner fails another server must take over cleanly.

steps.title: Store the operation log, with snapshots
steps.problem: An in-memory document is lost in a crash, and rewriting the whole document on every keystroke would be far too slow.
steps.fix: Every operation is appended to a durable log before it is acknowledged. Every few hundred operations, or after a pause in typing, the server writes a snapshot of the text. Opening a document loads the latest snapshot and replays the few operations after it. The log doubles as the version history, since any earlier state is a snapshot plus a prefix of the log.
steps.tradeoff: Nothing acknowledged is ever lost, a crashed server's replacement rebuilds the document in moments, and history comes for free. The log grows without end, so old operations are compacted into snapshots, and replay must be fast.

steps.title: Share cursors and presence without storing them
steps.problem: People want to see who is here and where they are typing, but cursor positions change many times a second and are worthless a moment later.
steps.fix: Presence information, such as cursor positions, selections and names, travels on a separate lightweight channel. It is never written to the log. It is throttled to a few updates per second per person and sent only to the others in the same document, and it expires when someone disconnects. Cursor positions are also transformed by incoming edits so they stay on the right letter.
steps.tradeoff: The live feel of seeing others costs little, and the durable log stays clean. Presence can be briefly out of date or lost, which is fine because the next update replaces it.

steps.title: Keep editing offline and when the connection drops
steps.problem: Connections break on trains and in lifts, and a person must not lose work or be locked out of typing.
steps.fix: The editor keeps a local copy and a queue of operations that the server has not acknowledged yet. Typing continues offline. When the connection returns the client sends the queue along with the server version it was based on, and the server transforms those operations against everything that happened in between, then sends back what the client missed. Operations carry ids, so one that was already received and acknowledged is not applied twice after a retry.
steps.tradeoff: People can work through outages and the merge is automatic. A long offline period can produce a surprising merge, so very large divergences are shown to the user, and the queue must be kept safe on the device until acknowledged.

failures.scenario: The document server for a busy document crashes
failures.impact: Its in-memory state and its open connections are lost, and editors cannot send changes.
failures.answer: The router assigns the document to another server, which loads the latest snapshot and replays the log. Editors reconnect and resend any unacknowledged operations with their ids, which the new server transforms and applies exactly once. People notice a pause of a second or two.

failures.scenario: Two people edit the same word at the same instant
failures.impact: Both operations were made against the same earlier text and refer to positions that overlap.
failures.answer: The server picks an order for the two operations and transforms the second against the first. Ties are broken by a fixed rule, such as the user id, so every copy decides the same way. Both people's edits survive and both see the same result.

failures.scenario: A client reconnects and resends operations the server has already received
failures.impact: Applying them again would type the text twice.
failures.answer: Each operation has a unique id made of the client and a counter, and the server records the highest counter it has seen from each client. A repeated operation is acknowledged again but not applied again.

failures.scenario: A hundred people open one document and all type
failures.impact: Each keystroke is broadcast to ninety-nine other people, and the document server is overloaded.
failures.answer: The server batches operations into small time slices, throttles presence updates, and beyond the hundred supported editors lets extra people join as read-only viewers, who need no transformation.

alternatives.title: How to merge simultaneous edits

options.name: Last write wins on the whole document
Operational transformation with a central server
options.pro: Compact, proven for text, and edits stay small
options.con: The transformation rules are hard to get right, and it needs a central sequencer

options.name: CRDTs (every character has a unique identity)
options.pro: No central ordering, and peers can merge directly, even offline
options.con: More metadata per character, and the document can grow with its history

alternatives.pick: Operational transformation with a server per document when a server is in the loop anyway. A CRDT when peer-to-peer or long offline editing matters most.

alternatives.title: How to route editors

options.name: Any server for any editor
options.con: No single order of operations for a document

options.name: All editors of a document on one server
options.pro: A single, simple ordering, and fast broadcasts
options.con: A hot document is limited by one machine, and a failover needs care

alternatives.pick: One owner server per document, chosen by consistent hashing.

alternatives.title: What to store

options.name: Only the latest text
options.con: No history, no undo for past sessions, and a crash can lose the last edits

options.name: Only the log of operations
options.con: Opening a long document means replaying everything

options.name: A log with periodic snapshots
options.pro: Durable, with fast opening, and full history
options.con: Two things to keep in step

alternatives.pick: A log with snapshots every few hundred operations.

alternatives.title: How undo should work

options.name: Revert to the previous document state
options.con: Would also undo other people's edits

options.name: Undo your own last operation, transformed past later edits
options.pro: Only your own changes are undone, as people expect
options.con: More complex, since the inverse must be transformed against everything since

alternatives.pick: Undo only your own operations, by transforming their inverses.

roles.label: Editors
roles.description: Browsers, with a local copy and a queue of unacknowledged edits.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The WebSocket gateway and the document router.

roles.label: Servers
roles.description: The document server and its transform engine.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The operation log, snapshots and the document store.

quiz.question: Two people edit one long document. The editor saves the whole text every 5 seconds and the server keeps the latest save. Alice and Bob each type a paragraph at the same time, and a few seconds later Bob's paragraph is gone. Which design fixes this?
options: Send each keystroke as a small operation to a server that orders it and transforms it against concurrent operations
Save every 500 milliseconds instead of every 5 seconds, so the window in which two saves collide is ten times smaller
Lock the whole document for whoever starts typing first, and release the lock after 10 seconds without typing
Merge the two saved texts on the server with a line-by-line three-way diff, the way source control merges branches
quiz.explanation: Small ordered operations mean nothing is overwritten and each copy converges. Saving more often still lets the last save win. A lock stops simultaneous typing, which the product needs, and a line diff reports conflicts when two people touch the same line and shows results late.

quiz.question: A document reads CAT, with positions counted from 0. Alice inserts X at position 0. At the same moment Bob deletes the letter at position 2, which is the T. The server orders Alice's operation first. What must Bob's operation become when it is applied to Alice's version XCAT so both copies agree?
options: Delete the letter at position 2, because the operation was valid when Bob made it and must be applied unchanged to the new text
Delete the letter at position 1, because Alice's insert shifts everything one place to the left of where it was before
Delete the letter at position 3, because the insertion before it moved the T one place further to the right of its old spot
Discard the delete and keep the T, because it conflicted with an operation the server ordered first
quiz.explanation: Alice's insert comes before the T, so the T now sits at position 3 and the delete must follow it. Applying position 2 would remove the A on one copy and the T on the other. Position 1 shifts the wrong way, because an insert before the T moves it to the right, not the left. Discarding the delete would lose Bob's edit, which transformation is meant to keep.

quiz.question: A note-taking product adds a mobile mode in which devices edit the same document for days with no connection to any server and sync directly with each other when they meet. The team uses operational transformation with one owner server per document today. What is the best choice for this mode?
options: Keep operational transformation, with each device queueing operations and sending them to the server when it is next online
Use a CRDT, where each character has a unique ordered identity and copies merge in any order
Use last write wins per paragraph with device timestamps, so that merges need no transformation rules
Elect one device as the sequencer for each document, and let it transform the operations of the others when they meet
quiz.explanation: Transformation needs one agreed order, and here no server or stable sequencer is reachable. A CRDT lets peers merge in any order and any number of times. Last write wins loses work, and a sequencer device may be the one that is offline.
